title: CPU, memory, storage and I/O
description: Understand how the CPU, memory, storage, and input/output systems work together.

data.text: Your computer is a busy city. The CPU is the factory that does all the work. Memory is the whiteboard where the factory writes quick notes. Storage is the filing cabinet where long-term records are kept. Input and output devices are the doors and windows through which data enters and leaves. Every program depends on how these four parts cooperate.

The Central Processing Unit (CPU) executes instructions from your programs. It has three main parts: the control unit fetches and decodes instructions, the arithmetic logic unit (ALU) performs math and comparisons, and registers hold tiny amounts of data for immediate use. Modern CPUs have multiple cores, allowing them to work on several tasks at once.

data.title: What the CPU actually does
items: Executes the instruction using the ALU or registers
Writes the result back to memory or registers

data.text: Computer memory, usually called RAM (Random Access Memory), stores data that the CPU is actively using. RAM is extremely fast but volatile — when the power turns off, everything in RAM disappears. Think of RAM as a desk: you spread out the papers you need right now so you can reach them quickly.

data.title: Volatile by design
data.text: RAM loses its contents when power is lost. This is not a flaw — it is a trade-off that makes RAM fast enough for the CPU to keep up.

Storage devices — hard drives (HDDs), solid-state drives (SSDs), and even older technologies — keep data permanently. Storage is much slower than RAM, which is why operating systems move only the data the CPU needs right now into RAM. When you open a file, the OS copies it from storage into memory.
Input and Output: Moving Data In and Out

Input devices (keyboard, mouse, network card, sensors) send data into the computer. Output devices (monitor, speakers, printer, network card) send data out. I/O is often the slowest part of any operation because mechanical devices and network signals are orders of magnitude slower than the CPU.

data.title: Reading a file from disk
data.content: When your program reads a file, data travels through every layer: storage device -> disk controller -> OS buffer -> RAM -> CPU cache -> CPU register.
data.code:
// C# example: reading a file triggers storage I/O
var text = await File.ReadAllTextAsync("data.txt");

data.caption: How the CPU, memory, and I/O interact
data.definition:
graph LR
    CPU -->|Reads/Writes| RAM
    RAM -->|Holds| Program
    CPU -->|Issues| IO[I/O Controller]
    IO -->|Reads/Writes| Disk
    IO -->|Reads/Writes| Network

data.text: Computers use multiple layers of memory, trading speed for size. The CPU has tiny, lightning-fast registers. Next comes CPU cache — still small but much larger than registers. Then RAM, which is bigger but slower. Finally, storage, which is huge but slowest. Good programmers write code that uses this hierarchy well by keeping hot data in faster memory.

items.question: Why is RAM slower than CPU cache?
items.answer: Cache memory is built directly into the CPU chip and uses a faster technology. RAM sits on a separate chip connected by a bus, so signals take longer to travel.

items.question: Does the CPU access storage directly?
items.answer: No. The CPU requests data through memory controllers and I/O subsystems. This indirection adds latency but allows many devices to share the same pathways.

items.question: What is throughput vs latency?
items.answer: Throughput is how much data moves per second. Latency is how long the first byte takes to arrive. SSDs have higher throughput than HDDs, but latency still matters for small random reads.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: The CPU executes instructions using registers and cache
RAM holds active data but loses it when powered off
Storage keeps data permanently but is much slower
I/O is usually the biggest performance bottleneck
data.takeaway: Understanding the memory hierarchy helps you write programs that avoid unnecessary disk access and make better use of CPU cache.
